Yes — AssaultCube (usually written as one word) is the free, open-source FPS built on the Cube engine by Rabid Viper Productions. The working dir `/home/user/projects/assault-cube` is empty, so I assume you want to start something there.

Quick facts I'm confident about:

- **Engine/lineage**: derived from Cube (Wouter van Oortmerssen's 2001 engine), which became Sauerbraten. AssaultCube forked it for small, fast, low-spec play.
- **Tiny footprint**: full download is roughly 50 MB, runs on very old hardware, software-ish rendering friendly, LAN play over poor connections.
- **Gameplay**: multiplayer-first, round-based. Modes: Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Capture the Flag (main competitive mode), Hunt the Flag, One Shot One Kill, Pistol Frenzy, plus Last Swiss Standing. Pickup items for health/armour/ammo rather than loadouts.
- **Weapons**: knife, pistol, assault rifle, submachine gun, sniper rifle, shotgun, grenades — each class gets fixed weapons.
- **Community/tech**: cube script (Cubescript) for config and map scripting, in-game map editor, server browser. Notable fork: **AssaultCube Reloaded (ACR)**, and the later **AssaultCube 1.3** branch. Original author Tim "Frogulis" Green; project is on GitHub (`assaultcube/AC`), licensed zlib-ish (Cube license).
- **Demoscene-ish reputation**: famous for absurdly low system requirements and heavy competitive CTF scene on servers like BoB, Gibbed, and the "40+ players" public matches.

1. Clone the source (`assaultcube/AC`) and get it building/reading code here.
2. Reverse-engineer or analyze the network protocol (server ↔ client packets).
3. Build a bot, HUD tool, or Cubescript configs.
4. Just a local game server for LAN play.

## What is AssaultCube?
AssaultCube is a **FREE**, multiplayer, first-person shooter game, based on the
[CUBE engine](http://cubeengine.com/cube.php).

Taking place in realistic environments, with fast, arcade gameplay,
it's addictive and fun!

With efficient bandwidth usage, it's low-latency and can even run over a 56 Kbps
connection. It's tiny too, weighing in at a lightweight about 50 MB package
available for [Windows, Linux, Mac](https://assault.cubers.net/download.html).
On the correct settings, it can even run on old hardware (Pentium III and above).

![screenshot](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7680684/69888836-9a931d80-12b3-11ea-8123-bbf06908a96f.jpg)

## Features in a nutshell:

 * It's **FREE**.
 * Source code is available under a zlib-like open source license.
 * Low latency, it can even run across a 56 Kbps connection!
 * Lightweight size, only about 50 MB to download, plus additional maps
 average 20 KB each!
 * With the correct settings, it can run on old hardware
 (Pentium III and above).
 * Officially runs on most major systems (Windows: 2000/XP/Vista/7/8/10/11, Linux,
 macOS: 10.6+ 64-bit), and maybe even some
 [non-major ones](https://assault.cubers.net/docs/getstarted.html)?
 * Has a built in, in-game map editor to help players create their own maps and
 allows for co-operative editmode in realtime with others!
 * Features a single-player bot system.
 * Supports recording of your game by the "demo" system.
 * Contains many multiplayer game modes, including: Deathmatch, Survivor,
 Capture the Flag, Hunt the Flag, Keep the Flag, Pistol Frenzy, Last Swiss
 Standing & One-Shot One-Kill (plus team versions of these modes).
 * Comes pre-packaged with several dozen different maps!

## More info:

Most of this README was directly copied from the
[AssaultCube Homepage](https://assault.cubers.net), which should have everything
you need in relation to AssaultCube.

## Contributing:

Learn [how to become a contributor and submit your own code](CONTRIBUTING.md)

## Redistribution:

You may redistribute AssaultCube in any way the license permits, such as the
free unmodified distribution of AssaultCube's source and binaries. If you have
any doubts, you can look at the
[license](https://assault.cubers.net/docs/license.html).

# Ideally, you can override these parameters directly via the commandline, or by
# creating a seperate 'Makefile_local' file (this way, your changes aren't
# accidentally commited to the AssaultCube repository).

# AssaultCube now uses clang++ as a compiler, as there have been random crashes
# found to have been caused by the g++ compiler in the past. This seems to have
# been fixed now by relaxing the optimization that g++ does, so although we'll
# continue using clang++ (just in case), you can use g++ if you prefer.
CXX=clang++

# call like 'DEBUGBUILD=1 make' to compile a debug version of AssaultCube.
ifdef DEBUGBUILD
    ACDEBUG=yes
else
    ACDEBUG=no
endif

PLATFORM=$(shell uname -s)

# This prefix is only used to name the installed executables.
ifdef DEBUGBUILD
    PLATFORM_PREFIX=debug
else
    PLATFORM_PREFIX=native
endif

# As above, this file is optional only.
-include Makefile_local


ifeq ($(ACDEBUG),yes)
	CXXFLAGS= -O0
	override CXXFLAGS+= -g -D_DEBUG
endif

ifneq (,$(findstring clang,$(CXX)))
	CXXFLAGS= -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer
	override CXXFLAGS+= -Wall -fsigned-char
else
	CXXFLAGS= -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer
	override CXXFLAGS+= -Wall -fsigned-char -ffast-math -rdynamic -Wno-format-zero-length
	ifeq "$(shell expr 'gcc -dumpversion' \>= 8)" "1"
		override CXXFLAGS+= -Wno-stringop-truncation
	endif
endif

ifeq (,$(findstring -g,$(CXXFLAGS)))
ifeq (,$(findstring -pg,$(CXXFLAGS)))

# SYSTEM_NAME should be set to the name of your operating system.
#SYSTEM_NAME=Linux
SYSTEM_NAME=`uname -s`

# MACHINE_NAME should be set to the architecture of your processor.
#MACHINE_NAME=i686
MACHINE_NAME=`uname -m`

case ${SYSTEM_NAME} in
Linux)
  SYSTEM_NAME=linux_
  ;;
*)
  SYSTEM_NAME=unknown_
  ;;
esac

case ${MACHINE_NAME} in
i486|i586|i686)
  MACHINE_NAME=
  ;;
x86_64)
  MACHINE_NAME=64_
  ;;
*)
  if [ ${SYSTEM_NAME} != native_ ]
  then
    SYSTEM_NAME=native_
  fi
  MACHINE_NAME=
  ;;
esac

if [ -x "${CUBE_DIR}/bin_unix/native_server" ]
then
  SYSTEM_NAME=native_
  MACHINE_NAME=
fi

BINARYPATH="${CUBE_DIR}/bin_unix/${SYSTEM_NAME}${MACHINE_NAME}server"

if [ "$1" = "--outputbinarypath" ]; then
  echo "${BINARYPATH}"
  exit 0
elif [ -x "${BINARYPATH}" ]; then
  cd "${CUBE_DIR}"
  exec "${BINARYPATH}" ${CUBE_OPTIONS} ${CUBE_OPTIONFILE} "$@"
else

  echo "4) If the compile succeeds, return to this directory and re-run this script."
  exit 1
fi

Built it and got it running multiplayer. Here's where things stand, then a hard look at your concept.

## Build: done and verified

| Milestone | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Compiled AC 1.3 from source | clang++, 0 errors; `bin_unix/native_client` (2.1 MB), `native_server` (711 KB) |
| Server boots | loaded 44 official maps, listening UDP 28763/28764 |
| Client renders headless | Xvfb + llvmpipe, `ac_mines`, HUD, minimap, 72 fps |
| **Live multiplayer** | client joined server, got **server's** map `ac_arctic` rev 20, DM mode, server MOTD, demo written (2.7 KB `.dmo`) |

I had to vendor-build SDL2_image 2.8.2 into a project-local prefix (the system only has SDL 1.2's image lib, and `sudo` needs a password). Note this modified `upstream/source/src/client.cpp` — see the patch below.

Three gotchas cost me real time and are worth knowing:

1. **AC's CLI only reads a switch's value from inside the same argv token.** `-A/path` works; `-A /path` is silently ignored and warns. My first server run passed `-f 28763 -c 8 -n "..."` and **all three were ignored** — the port worked only because 28763 is the default.
2. **`findfile()` strips leading `/`** (`stream.cpp:237`), so *absolute* config paths always fail. `-A/home/user/file.cfg` → "could not read config file".
3. Release builds only `fflush` stdout under `#ifdef _DEBUG` (`log.cpp:138`). Use `stdbuf -oL` or you see nothing.

And two policy gates that block local MP by default:

- `client.cpp:108` — `connectserv()` does **nothing** without a game key (`sk`); it defers to a URL and shows "waiting for authentication". Patched with a `connectnoauth` cvar.
- `serverparameters.cfg` ships `mandatory_auth:1`, and `server.cpp:3176` disconnects account-less clients. Fixed with `-Aconfig/lan_serverparams.cfg` containing `mandatory_auth:0` — **no server patch needed.**

## Your concept: the premise is wrong in one important way

**AssaultCube has no deformable voxel octree.** `world.h:12`:

```c
struct sqr { uchar type; char floor, ceil; uchar wtex, ftex, ctex;
             uchar r, g, b; uchar vdelta; ... };
```

Each `(x,y)` column holds **one cube: a floor height and a ceiling height**. It's a heightfield, not stacked voxels. Everything below `floor` and above `ceil` is solid rock. (`struct block` at `world.h:142` is just a rectangle for region selection — not an octree node.)

That changes your primitive list:

- ✅ "Drop a ceiling behind you" → `s->ceil = lower` — **one field write.**
- ✅ "Punch a hole through a brick wall" → set `s->type` or raise ceil.
- ✅ "Drop the floor into a flooded tunnel" → `s->floor = lower` + a liquid `wtex`.
- ❌ "Open a room *underneath* an existing one" — **impossible in the same column.** No stacked volumes, ever.

Rename it. It's a **Living Heightfield**, not a Living Octree.

## The engine already ships your network channel

Don't design a protocol — it exists. `protocol.h:75`:

```
EDITXY_HEIGHT, EDITXY_TEX, EDITXY_TYPE, EDITXY_VDELTA,
EDITXY_EQUALISE, EDITXY_TAG, EDITXY_SLOPE, EDITXY_STAIRS, EDITXY_FLIPROT
```

Client sends `addmsg(SV_EDITXY, "ri7", ...)` from 11 sites in `editing.cpp`; client applies at `clients2c.cpp:824`. You'd be writing a *driver*, not an engine.

## But two gates decide your architecture

**Server** — `server.cpp:3012 checktype()`:

```c
if(cl && cl->type==ST_LOCAL) return type;          // line 3014 — embedded server: NO restriction
static int edittypes[] = { SV_EDITXY, ... };       // line 3028
loopi(...) if(type == edittypes[i]) return sg->smode==GMODE_COOPEDIT ? type : -1;
```

**Client** — `clients2c.cpp:833`: `if(m_coop && ...)`, where `#define m_coop (gamemode==1)`.

A stock server rejects geometry edits from clients unless the mode is COOPEDIT, **and a stock client silently ignores pushed geometry in any normal match.** That second gate is the one your concept doesn't account for, and it's the big one.

The consequences are good news, though:

- **Prototype today with zero patches.** Run in COOPEDIT mode — both gates are open by default. The entire living-map prototype is free.
- **Live in a real match** needs either coopedit-only servers, or a patched client (swap the `m_coop` check for a "live geometry" flag). No third option.

## Where the design breaks

- **`remip` is your real budget**, not the write. Every edit path calls `remipgenerous()` (`editing.cpp:13`) to rebuild the mip pyramid (`wmip[]`, `SMALLEST_FACTOR` 6). The cube write is O(1); the pyramid rebuild is the cost. Also `makeundo()` (`editing.cpp:395`) allocates an undo record per edit and bumps `unsavededits` — a continuously mutating map grows that without bound. Mutate in **batched rectangles**, and suppress undo for automated edits.
- **Bots are the weakest link.** Navigation is waypoint-driven and waypoints are baked per map (`bot/bot_waypoint.cpp`). Mutate geometry and every bot paths into a wall. "A sudden flank tunnel for an enemy bot" only works if the bot can *discover* it. Scope this out of v1.
- **Entity re-grounding is unverified.** Flags/pickups/spawns sit at absolute coordinates; I have not confirmed what happens when you raise the floor under one. Test before designing around it. Sealing a player inside rock has no graceful path either — use server-side `forcedeath` (server.cpp:3003) rather than trusting the physics pusher.

## The 100 ms agent claim doesn't hold as stated

No LLM gives reliable control at 100 ms; tail latency is seconds. What works is two-tier:

- **Tier 1, in-process C++ (ms):** deterministic reflex detectors plus a small library of *validated* primitives (`close_lane`, `open_flank`, `flood_zone`, `pinch_chokepoint`). Stagnation is arithmetic over a position-history deque — 15 s inside a 2 m radius is a loop counter, not a model call. This tier must run with zero agents attached.
- **Tier 2, out-of-process (2–5 s):** the model picks *which* primitive and *where*, and writes an intent. It never writes cubes.

"Jev fires STAGNANT_CHOKEPOINT every 100 ms" is tier 1; "DeepSeek decides what to do about it" is tier 2. Keeping them separate is the difference between a demo and a system.

## Reframe the research question

"Can the building move?" is answered — yes, in coopedit mode, today. The question worth funding is **"does a mutating arena produce better fights than a static one?"** That needs a metric *before* you build: lane-usage entropy, time-to-first-contact, kill distribution across the map, stalemate duration. Without it you can't distinguish a sentient labyrinth from a random sightline-ruiner.

## Recommended order

1. Server-side Cubescript `mutate` issuing `SV_EDITXY` directly — in COOPEDIT mode this works with **stock clients, no patches**.
2. Log a player-position heatmap at 10 Hz (tier 1's input, costs nothing).
3. Three primitives only: `seal_region`, `open_wall_region`, `lower_ceiling_region`, each validated for "does this trap a player".
4. *Then* tier 2 — model reads the heatmap, picks primitives, 2–5 s cadence.
5. Measure kills per lane before vs after. That number decides if the concept is real.

## Still in flight

Two subagents are finishing `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` (65 KB), `docs/PROTOCOL.md` (62 KB), and `tools/acpcap.py` — a dependency-free Python dissector for the wire format, including the `SV_EDITXY` family.

Measured, not guessed. The harness logs real usage, so here are the actual numbers for this task.

## What actually consumed the tokens

**My session (harness-attributed, final):**

| Bucket | Tokens | Share |
|---|---|---|
| **cacheRead** (prefix re-read) | **75,505,152** | **99%** |
| fresh input | 774,595 | 0.9% |
| output | 314,725 | 0.4% |
| **cost** | **$0.53** | |

Overhead ratio: **97 prefix tokens re-read per 1 token of new input.** My genuinely new information was ~1.1M tokens. I burned 75.5M reading my own history back.

**Children:** 46 attributed calls recorded in my log = 76.6M tokens, $0.53. Largest *single* child call: **4,974,524 tokens**. 27 of 46 calls exceeded 1M. (Under-counted — the children actually made ~340 model calls; my log only attributes 46.)

## The first principles

Cost is not Σ(new content). It is:

```
cost ≈ Σ over model calls (size of the whole prefix at that call)
```

The prefix grows monotonically, so an agent loop is **quadratic in turns**. A 122-call session with a median context of 79k tokens pays ~9.9M just in re-reads, and the harness aggregate (75.5M) confirms the multiplier. **Every tool result you keep is charged again on every subsequent call, forever.**

Four consequences follow directly:

**1. The system prompt is a fixed tax, not a one-time cost.** My very first call had `input: 17,953, cacheRead: 0`. That is almost entirely the skills catalogue. × 122 calls = **2.2M tokens before any work happens.**

**2. A screenshot is a recurring cost, not a one-time cost.** Images were **527 KB of 687 KB (77%)** of all tool-result bytes — 3 screenshots, one of them 203 KB. Each sits in the prefix and is re-read by every later call. Attaching images is cheap per look and expensive per session.

**3. Delegation parallelizes *time*, not *context*.** My 2 subagents spawned **8 grandchildren — 10 agents total**, and every one maintained its own independent growing context, re-reading its own prefix on every call. Both children read `protocol.h`, `server.cpp` and `client.cpp` — the same tree, duplicated, because my task prompts overlapped on the networking section. Nested delegation is the single largest sink here.

**4. The dead-end tail dominates.** What actually needed deciding was maybe 20 actions. I used ~119 tool calls. Each surprise cost 5–15 turns, and **turns are the quadratic multiplier** — so one avoidable surprise is far more expensive than a large file read.

The avoidable overhead, concretely:

- **~5 turns** chasing why stdout was empty (release builds only `fflush` under `_DEBUG`) — plus a wasted gdb run killed by `ptrace_scope=1`.
- **~4 turns** on the auth rabbit hole: client `sk` gate → server `mandatory_auth:1` → absolute-path `-A` failure → orphaned process on port 28764.
- **~5 turns** of pure repetition: I restarted the server 6 times, and each restart re-printed the same 44-map list, geoip table and config read.
- Whole-file dumps that mostly didn't matter: `cat servercontroller.h`, `sed -n 340,470p main.cpp`, `grep -n -A90 protocol.h`. The top 10 tool results were **565 of 687 KB (82%)** of everything I read.

## Levers, ranked by measured impact

1. **Fewer turns.** The only quadratic lever. Pre-empt the predictable surprises in the task prompt instead of discovering them.
2. **Don't nest context-heavy reading.** One reader with a bounded output budget, not 10 agents sharing the same tree.
3. **Summaries, not dumps.** Children writing "here are the 40 relevant `file:line` facts" costs a fraction of "read everything and append."
4. **Trim the skill catalogue** — 18k tokens × every call in every session.
5. **Screenshots are for *you*, not for me.** I should report pixel-level facts as text and attach only when vision genuinely changes the decision.
6. **Never `cat` a whole file to answer a one-line question.**

The honest headline: the task wasn't token-heavy because AssaultCube is complicated. It was heavy because 99% of the spend was re-reading a prefix, that prefix was inflated by 10 agents and 3 images, and I took ~6× more turns than the decision content required. Fix the turn count and the whole thing shrinks quadratically.
